extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newspaper editors, students of journalism and public opinion, and social scientists interested in press standards
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for judging how newspapers select, frame, and present news, and for understanding the limits of the press in conveying truth. Emphasis on editorial selection, source reliability, stereotypes, institutional context, and the distinction between news and truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: News requires an overt signal
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The facts do not become news, until the workers organize and make a demand… they have normally to wait for a signal in the shape of an overt act.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events that are remote, complex, or ongoing typically only become reportable news when an overt, observable action (demand, strike, summons for police, disorder) occurs; reporters and readers rely on these signals to notice and categorize events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report events in relation to reader's experience
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The easiest way is to let the news be uncovered by the overt act, and to describe the event as the story of interference with the reader's life. That is where his attention is first aroused, and his interest most easily enlisted.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and reporters frame stories to show how incidents affect readers (inconvenience, shortages, threats to their jobs), because rapid reader identification is necessary to secure attention; this explains frequent emphasis on immediate, personal impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of stereotypes to make distant facts intelligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Distant or unfamiliar facts are ‘animated’ by stereotypes so readers can ‘translate (them) at once into our parallel facts.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalism relies on conventional labels and stereotypes (e.g., calling a plumbers’ association a 'combine' or a 'group of leading business men') to cue readers’ reactions quickly; this is a common technique but can distort nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial selection governed by probable interest and practical constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Every bulletin requires a swift but complicated judgment…played up or played down according to its probable interest for the public…final page is of a definite size, must be ready at a precise moment…there can be only a certain number of captions.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of what to publish and how prominently depends on time pressure, space limits, deadlines, legal risks (libel), and the editor’s estimate of audience interest, not purely on objective importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardization and routine are necessary to produce a daily paper
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Without standardization, without stereotypes, without routine judgments, without a fairly ruthless disregard of subtlety, the editor would soon die of excitement…The thing could not be managed at all without systematization.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic formats, conventions, and shortcuts are functional necessities for newspapers to meet deadlines and offer a predictable product; they economize time and reduce some risks at the cost of subtlety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopted reporting models shape the press universally
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Certain dailies…took the lead in securing news, and the way that news was presented became a model for the whole press…that model came from the English press…’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When some papers develop reporting techniques (e.g., war reporting), those models are adopted broadly; reliance on a few foreign or leading sources can standardize coverage and propagate particular framings or biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess and be responsible for the reliability of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘If there is one subject on which editors are most responsible it is in their judgment of the reliability of the source.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must judge source credibility and avoid amplifying unreliable claims; do not assert uncertain facts definitively (example: instead of 'Lenin Dead' use 'Helsingfors says Lenin is dead').

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish the function of news from the function of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The function of news is to signalize an event, the function of truth is to bring to light the hidden facts, to set them into relation with each other, and make a picture of reality on which men can act.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate news (a signal about events) with comprehensive truth; most news cannot by itself provide the deeper, corroborated account required for reliable understanding or decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision of news tracks the precision of recorded events
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The news, as we have seen, is precise in proportion to the precision with which the event is recorded.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective, recordable events (e.g., bankruptcy filings) allow precise reporting; complex social causes without exact records invite multiple plausible narratives and weaker tests of accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid presenting opinion or rumor as settled fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Where objective tests are absent, ‘the rest is in the journalist's own discretion…his version of the truth is only his version.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When covering matters lacking objective records, reporters should make the provisional nature of their accounts clear and avoid implying a unique, demonstrable truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press is too frail to carry the whole burden of democracy’s information needs
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The press is not constituted to furnish from one edition to the next the amount of knowledge which the democratic theory of public opinion demands…It is too frail to carry the whole burden of popular sovereignty.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not judge newspapers by the unrealistic standard that they should supply comprehensive expertise on all public problems; institutions and organized record-keeping are required to support informed public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of news is an index of social organization
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The better the institutions, the more all interests concerned are formally represented, the more issues are disentangled, the more objective criteria are introduced, the more perfectly an affair can be presented as news.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improved institutional record, formal representation, and objective criteria make it easier for the press to report complex affairs accurately; poor institutions expose journalism to distortion and exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting chaos and distant events is especially error-prone
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The hardest thing to report is chaos…This put the formulating of Russian news at its source…into the hands of censors and propagandists…they created…stereotypes so evocative of hate and fear.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When access is limited (censorship, language barriers) and the situation is chaotic, reporting will often rely on filtered, second-hand accounts that can produce stereotyped, propagandistic narratives; exercise caution and caveat attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: News tends to record overt phases, not the intangible causes
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The bulletins from the scene of action will note the trouble that arose from the assertion, rather than the reasons which led to it. The reasons are intangible.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect routine news accounts to emphasize visible incidents (strikes, disorders) over their complex causes (working conditions, economic pressures); deeper explanation often requires investigative work and institutional records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors will prefer indisputable facts when stakes are dangerous
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘These difficulties combined make for uncertainty in the editor when there are dangerous issues at stake, and cause him naturally to prefer the indisputable fact and a treatment more readily adapted to the reader's interest.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In tense or risky contexts, editors are likely to emphasize verifiable, simple facts and familiar framings rather than complex, controversial analyses; this preference affects what becomes news and how it is presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivated reader partisanship constrains editorial change
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Many a newspaper finds that, having honestly evoked the partisanship of its readers, it can not easily, supposing the editor believes the facts warrant it, change position.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once a paper has built a partisan readership through consistent framing, practical and commercial pressures make abrupt editorial reversals difficult; transitions must be handled delicately or the topic may simply be allowed to fade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press should make the uncertainty of social truth plain and promote organized intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘It is possible and necessary for journalists to bring home to people the uncertain character of the truth on which their opinions are founded, and by criticism and agitation to prod social science into making more usable formulations of social facts…The press, in other words, can fight for the extension of reportable truth.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists have a responsibility to indicate uncertainty, avoid misleading definitiveness, and to advocate for better institutional record-keeping and social-scientific inquiry that will make deeper truths more reportable.
